body.text: After months of keeping New Delhi at arm’s length, Nepal’s Balendra Shah government is discovering both the appeal and the political risks of drawing it closer.

Formed after the March 2026 elections, the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) government did not start on the right foot with the southern neighbor. First, new Prime Minister Balendra Shah declined a one-on-one meeting with then-Indian Ambassador Naveen Shrivastava, in keeping with his policy of not meeting any foreign officials.

What rankled more with the Indians was his subsequent refusal to meet India’s Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, who was coming to Kathmandu carrying Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s formal invitation for Shah to visit India. Misri’s trip was called off. India — which continues to emphasize its “unique” relations with Nepal that are unlike its ties with any other country — saw this as a snub, and a breach of trust.

Those were not the only irritants in bilateral ties. The new government in Kathmandu started taxing goods bought by Nepali nationals in Indian border towns, hampering the business of these hubs that rely on Nepali buyers. Entry of Indian vehicles into Nepal was also restricted.
That was the state of affairs for the first five or six months of the Shah government.
But the tide seems to have turned and the government now appears keen to woo the Indians. At the forefront of this effort is Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle.

Even before the March elections, as a top RSP leader, Wagle had repeatedly visited New Delhi with a message that should his party come to power, it would go the extra mile to protect Indian interests.

Of late, Wagle seems to have gotten the government’s green light to boldly assert that the era of “anti-India nationalism” in Nepal is over and his government is ready to turn over a new leaf with the southern neighbor.

Curiously, he and his government also sound accommodative of India’s self-declared red lines. In a recent interview with The Hindu, the Nepali minister said that Nepal now accepts that India’s refusal to buy hydropower from Nepali projects with Chinese investment is a “new geopolitical reality.”

Yet the finance minister is only laying the ground for Shah’s much-awaited India visit in the third week of November. Home Minister Sudan Gurung has also contributed to this effort, outlining potential areas of bilateral cooperation in a recent op-ed. Big deals are being planned during Shah’s visit.

But for any government in Kathmandu, close relations with India come with both costs and benefits. The obvious benefit is that New Delhi pulls many strings in Kathmandu, and it can make life difficult for a Nepali prime minister it does not like. The latest overtures of his government toward India suggest Shah does not want to be one of them.

If Shah can convince New Delhi to, say, secure an additional air route for Nepal during his India trip, it will be a new feather in his bhadgaule cap — and a tangible achievement for his nationalist base back home.

Yet there are also costs of closer ties with India. Whatever Wagle says, the days of anti-India nationalism in Nepal are far from over — as is also evident in the fierce criticism of his remarks in Nepali intellectual circles. Nepalis continue to be suspicious of the oft-meddling regional hegemon that has thrice imposed crippling blockades on the landlocked country.

Shah got an overwhelming mandate, and he can afford to use some of his political capital to push through vital projects with India. But irrespective of how well Shah’s India trip goes, there will still be irritants in bilateral ties.

For instance, a major disagreement remains between Kathmandu and New Delhi on an old border dispute. After India and China unilaterally opened the Lipulekh pass — a trijunction point between the three countries — for trade earlier this year, Kathmandu swiftly dispatched diplomatic notes to New Delhi and Beijing. This issue could again flare up as both New Delhi and Beijing seem to be in a mood to overrule Nepal’s objections and give continuity to their trade through the pass.

It will be hard for the Shah government to stand firm on Lipulekh — something that is in keeping with the Nepali public sentiment — while also pursuing closer cooperation with India. If it does not handle the issue well, a “compromise” on territorial integrity to secure favorable trade terms could even be portrayed domestically as a surrender to the regional hegemon.
Then there is China. The government has signaled that closer ties with India are worth paying the price of narrowing the space for Chinese investment in Nepali hydropower.

Yet if the government pushes Beijing too far through such gestures, it will violate a central tenet of Nepali foreign policy: maintenance of a delicate balance between Beijing and New Delhi. There will thus be a strong opposition to an overt India tilt.

In the end, Shah and his ministers would do well to avoid making sweeping claims that old constraints in India-Nepal ties have disappeared or that the anti-India nationalism in Nepal has run its course. Nurturing this complicated relationship requires sustained diplomacy and setting of realistic expectations. Only then can Nepal protect its interests.
